title: Showcase: one line of Python
summary: Run the week 11 badge in Python for the family, explain one real line of code, and say what comes next season.

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.body:
Every Python badge in this course was typed from the same steps. Now make yours the only one like it: add one behavior no step told you to make. It opens your demo, so build it before the family watches.

1. Plug the micro:bit into the laptop with the USB cable, and open https://python.microbit.org. If your badge code is not already there, click `Open` and pick the `.hex` file you saved in week 11.
2. Pick one new behavior for the badge. Small is fine, as long as it is yours.
3. Sketch it in your Problem Notebook or on any paper: what starts it, and what happens then.
4. Set a timer for 15 minutes. Type it, click `Send to micro:bit`, and test it on the board.
5. Stuck? Climb the ladder from Find the answer yourself: the last line of the error, then the `Reference` tab, then Ask, then a grown-up.
6. Click `Save`, and keep the new `.hex` file next to your week 11 one.
7. Write "What is new about mine" in two or three sentences: what it does, and why you wanted it. You read them out first when the demo starts.
8. In this week's Maker's Log, start your answer to "What did you make?" with those same sentences. They stay with your photo and video in your portfolio.

Three sparks, just to get you thinking. They are not the assignment:

Spark: Score keeper. Each press of button A adds one point, and button B scrolls the score.

Spark: Launch countdown. One press counts down 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 on the display, then shows a picture of your own.

Spark: Tiny flipbook. Three pictures you draw yourself, shown one after another, so something moves across the badge.

The best idea is one that is not on this list. An entry in your Problem Notebook might spark it.

Trick: Make a number move. Your programs are full of numbers. Keep one in a variable and change it while the program runs, the way `step = step + 5` grew your spiral in week 10.

Not working when the timer ends? Show it anyway. Say what it should do, read out the error, and say what you tried. That is a real demo too.

You are done when: your badge does one thing no step told you to build, the same way twice in a row, and your sentences are written.
checklist: No step told me to build this
I sketched it on paper before I typed it
It works the same way twice in a row
I wrote what is new about mine, in two or three sentences
I showed it first, before the rest of the demo

figure.alt: The showcase layout: the micro:bit badge with its battery running next to a laptop screen showing the Python code, an arrow pointing from the badge toward the line being pointed at on screen. Text below lists the demo order: say it, show it, point at a line, say what's next.

items.s: say it, show it, point at a line, say what's next

steps.title: Run the Python badge
steps.body:
Set the badge up before the family is watching, so your new behavior, name scrolling, the heartbeat and the button A happy face are already working, and clip on the battery pack.

Run the demo:

1. Read your "What is new about mine" sentences out loud, then show your new behavior running.
2. Say what the rest of the badge does, then show it: your name scrolls, the heart beats, and button A shows the happy face.
3. Open the Python code and point at one line you understand, like `while True:`, `sleep(500)`, or `if button_a.was_pressed():`. Say in your own words what that line does and why it is there.
4. Say one sentence: what would you build next season, the badge, the robot, or something new.

If the board shows a scrolling error instead of your program, read the line number out loud to the family. Show them the exact word or missing colon at that line. That still counts as a real demo.

steps.title: Build it again, no help
steps.body:
The one-line spec: `import turtle`, make a turtle named `t`, then a `for` loop that runs 4 times, with its lines indented four spaces: `t` goes forward 100, then turns right 90; `turtle.done()` is the last line.

Give it a real, focused 15 minutes. Set a timer, and see if you can beat it with the family watching. Before the timer starts, a grown-up opens Thonny, closes any file it reopened by itself, such as `shapes.py`, and clicks `File`, then `New`. Only that empty file should be open: no saved project, no notes. When Thonny asks where to save as you run it, call it `square.py`, never `turtle.py`.

If you truly get stuck, use `Jump to a different week` to go back to week 10, open the `Build` card, and read the guide once. If you do, write down which block, line or step you had forgotten.
checklist: I built it in 15 minutes or less, with only Thonny open
My turtle t draws the square, and it closes after four repeats
Every line inside the loop is indented four spaces under the for line
I did not look at my saved week 10 code
If I opened the old guide, I wrote down which step I had forgotten

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A short video of the whole demo, your new behavior first, then the pointed-at line and any error recovery, or a photo of the badge running with the code on screen.

extras.title: Point at two lines, not just one
extras.body:
Most demos only point at one line. Point at two, and connect them.

1. Before the family watches, open your Python code from week 11.
2. Pick a second line, different from the one you already planned to explain.
3. Write one sentence for what that second line does, in your own words.
4. Write one sentence for how the two lines work together.
5. During the demo, point at both lines and say both sentences out loud.

What to notice: most single lines of code only make sense next to another line.

extras.title: Say what happens next
extras.body:
If you kept building next season, what would you want your badge or robot to do?

Decide on one idea for something you would build next.

It must build on something real from this season, the badge, the dice, or the robot.
It must have one number you would want to choose by testing, even if unbuilt.
It must be said out loud to someone in your house, during or after the demo.

Sketch your idea on paper first.

How to know it works: someone else can repeat your idea back to you in their own words.

extras.title: The battery's push, one more time
extras.body:
Find out whether the same battery pack from week 4 still gives the same voltage now.

1. Predict first: guess how many volts the multimeter will read across the battery pack you used back in week 4. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Set a multimeter to measure DC volts.
3. Touch the two probes to the battery pack's wires and read the number.
4. Write down today's number next to your week 4 number, if you saved it.

Compare: is today's number close to week 4's number, lower, or about the same?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why a battery's push fades a little more with every week of use.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
